text: Every ML project starts as a notebook: load some data, train a model, get a promising number. That's a real result, but it isn't production ML — it's a single, manual, unrepeatable experiment. MLOps exists to turn that one-off into a repeatable pipeline, and the shape of that pipeline is always the same five stages: data, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor.

Data preparation pulls raw data from its source, cleans it, validates it against an expected schema, and splits it into training, validation, and test sets — as code, not a manual spreadsheet export. Training takes that data plus a set of hyperparameters and produces a model artifact, logging every metric as it goes. Evaluation then scores that model against held-out data and checks it against a gate before anything is allowed to move forward.

Written as code, the whole thing is just a sequence of function calls: prepare the data, train, evaluate, and check the result against the currently deployed model's score. Only if the new model clears that gate does it get deployed — rolled out gradually with the same canary or blue/green patterns you already know from application deployments. Everything here is repeatable and versioned, which is exactly what a notebook experiment never was.

Deployment is not the finish line. Once a model is live, monitoring watches its real-world accuracy and the statistical shape of incoming data, looking for drift — the point where production conditions have diverged enough from training time that accuracy is silently slipping. Critically, a drift alert doesn't end the pipeline; it loops straight back to stage one, pulling fresh data and kicking off a retrain automatically.

That feedback loop is the entire point. A notebook proves an idea exactly once, with no versioning and no safety checks before anything ships. A pipeline proves it again and again — on a schedule, on fresh data, or on demand — and it's the same discipline you already learned for CI/CD and GitOps in course twelve, just applied to models instead of application code.

You now have the full five-stage shape of the ML lifecycle. Next, lesson eighteen goes deep on the stage that makes every one of those training runs reproducible and comparable in the first place: experiment tracking and model registries, and why logging every hyperparameter and metric matters just as much as the training run itself.
